headline_hi: पहाड़ों के लिए उड़ने वाली कार
summary_en: Very inspiring news has emerged from Almora district of Uttarakhand. Ravi Tamta, a resident of Kaflikhan village, has made a unique invention. Ravi, the son of a mechanic, did not hold any engineering degree. He learned technology from the internet and developed the prototype of a flying car. It used to take hours to reach the hospital on the winding mountain roads. To solve this very problem of medical emergencies, he worked hard for thirteen years. This electric flying vehicle has been named 'Hapida Skynex'. This vehicle can take off directly upwards and also land without a runway. Its first test was conducted at the Army helipad in Almora in the month of August. This electric vehicle successfully flew in the air for about one minute. This technology will prove to be a boon for patients in remote hilly areas.

lead.title: ‘I Had No Engineering Degree’: Almora Mechanic’s Son Learnt From the Internet & Built a Flying Car
lead.summary: Flying cars are once again taking over the internet, with Tesla’s plans fuelling conversations about a future where people could travel through the air instead of sitting in traffic. But in Almora, Uttarakhand, an innovator has spent 13 years working towards a similar idea, driven by a problem much closer to home. Ravi Tamta grew up in the mountains of Kaflikhan village near Jageswar Dham, where reaching a hospital could mean hours on winding roads. He began wondering if there was another way to travel through the hills, one that did not depend on roads or require an airport. Inspired by the challenges of reaching hospitals in the hills, Ravi Tamta spent 13 years developing a flying vehicle that can take off and land vertically. Photograph: ( Zee News) That question led him to build HAPIDA SKYNeX, an electric flying vehicle prototype that can take off and land vertically. After years of experiments, the vehicle completed its maiden test flight in August, taking off from an army helipad in Almora and remaining airborne for nearly a minute. A mountain problem sparked the idea For people living in hilly regions, distance is not always measured in kilometres. Winding roads and difficult terrain can turn a relatively short journey into a long trip, particularly when someone needs medical attention. Tamta began exploring whether a flying vehicle could help people cover such distances faster. His idea was to develop a vehicle that could rise vertically, travel over difficult terrain, and land without needing a runway. View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Better India (@thebetterindia) The aim is to make air travel more accessible in hilly regions, particularly during medical emergencies and in areas that are difficult to reach by road. headline_hi: घूमने वाली सीट से आसान सफ़र
headline_en: Easy travel with a swivel seat
summary_en: Two engineers from Bengaluru have made travel extremely easy for persons with disabilities. Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre started a company named 'True Assistive Technology'. They have created a special swivel car seat named 'TurnPlus'. This seat rotates up to ninety degrees towards the car door. Because of this, passengers can be seated in the car without any trouble. Rashmi Sampat from Bengaluru lives with her sixteen-year-old daughter Deeksha. Deeksha is battling a disease called Spinal Muscular Atrophy. Earlier, seating Deeksha in the car was an exhausting task. With the help of this new seat, their family traveled from Bengaluru to Kanyakumari. They completed this long journey of one thousand kilometers very comfortably. The company has helped more than one thousand people so far. This technology is proving useful for patients with conditions like paralysis and Parkinson's.

lead.title: This Bengaluru Couple’s Swivel Car Seat Has Helped 1000+ People With Disabilities Travel Again
lead.summary: "Earlier, it was very difficult for me," says Bengaluru resident Rashmi Sampath, recalling every family outing with her 16-year-old daughter, Deeksha, who has spinal muscular atrophy. "She weighs 55 kilograms, and lifting her into the car was exhausting. But now, since the seat rotates 90 degrees, it is very comfortable." The difference has been more than convenience. A journey that once demanded careful planning, physical effort, and frequent compromises has become something the family can look forward to. Last year, they drove nearly 1,000 kilometres from Bengaluru to Kanyakumari without the travel itself becoming an obstacle. "She was very comfortable throughout," Rashmi says. "We took just two breaks. She could even sleep on the seat. Earlier, we couldn't have imagined travelling such a long distance like this." For millions of Indians living with disabilities or age-related mobility challenges, the hardest part of a journey often begins before the vehicle even starts moving. Getting into a car can require multiple people, unsafe lifting techniques, or simply deciding that the trip isn't worth the effort. It is this overlooked challenge that Bengaluru-based TRUE Assistive Technology set out to address. Founded by engineers Naina Padaki and Anand Kutre, the company designs assistive mobility solutions, including swivel seats, portable ramps, transfer systems, and wheelchair-accessible vehicle modifications, that make everyday travel safer and more accessible.  TurnPlus rotates towards the car door, making it easier for passengers to get in and out with less physical strain. headline_hi: दुनिया का सबसे ऊंचा विंड टरबाइन
summary_en: The world's tallest wind turbine has been completed in Germany. This massive structure has been erected in the Schipkau area of eastern Germany. The total height of this turbine has reached three hundred and sixty-five meters. After Berlin's TV tower, it is the second tallest structure in Germany. It has been built with the help of the company 'Gicon' and the government agency 'SPRIND'. At such a high altitude, wind speed remains very fast and steady. The company says it can generate twice as much electricity as a conventional turbine. The production capacity of this turbine has been set at three point eight megawatts. For construction at such a height, a telescoping tower was used instead of a crane. The inner tower was raised up and safely locked within the lattice structure. Company CEO Jochen Grossmann called it a major achievement for his team.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: World’s tallest wind turbine reaches 1,197 feet in Germany
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM The world’s tallest wind turbine just reached full height in Germany. GICON ‘s pilot turbine in Schipkau, eastern Germany, now stands 365 meters (1,197 feet) tall from base to blade tip, making it Germany’s second-tallest structure after Berlin’s TV tower . Official commissioning is set for November. Higher altitude, stronger winds Higher up, winds are faster and more reliable. That translates to more hours of generation per year, and GICON says its design could produce roughly twice the electricity of a conventional turbine with the same rotor diameter. One thing to flag: that’s a claim about cumulative generation over time, not rated power. The turbine’s rated capacity is 3.8 megawatts; future versions are designed to go past seven. The rotor hub sits 300 meters (984 feet) above the ground. Building that high required rethinking construction. A crane capable of reaching 1,197 feet wasn’t realistic, so GICON used a telescoping tower instead. A specialized lifting system raised an inner tower through a surrounding lattice structure, then locked it at full extension. “365 meters – this is an overwhelming moment for our entire team,” said GICON founder and CEO Jochen Großmann. “What was long a challenging idea and then an equally challenging construction project now stands as a globally unique facility in Schipkau.” A second tier for existing wind farms GICON and its funder, Germany’s Federal Agency for Disruptive Innovation (SPRIND), aren’t pitching these turbines as replacements for existing wind farms. summary_en: Teenagers around the world are stepping forward to tackle the plastic crisis. In a school in Singapore, two thousand students used seventy-two thousand items made of thermocol and other plastics every year. For a solution, they joined the 'Unplastify Challenge'. In this initiative by the Latin American organization Unplastify, fifteen to sixteen-year-old teenagers design solutions. The students of Singapore secured first place by running a campaign for reusable lunch boxes. Over the past eight years, more than three thousand students from four hundred schools across twenty-five countries have joined this campaign. They have helped prevent seventy-two tons of plastic. In Chile, students saved four kilograms of plastic by making biodegradable glitter. In Costa Rica, natural loofahs were adopted instead of plastic sponges. In Turkey, teenagers have explored eco-friendly alternatives to medical equipment like plastic gloves.

lead.title: Teenagers Worldwide Are Tackling the Plastics Crisis
lead.summary: W hen students in Singapore looked around their school cafeteria, they could see a problem shared all over the world: Single-use Styrofoam was ubiquitous. They soon learned that the school’s 2,000 students used 72,000 pieces of Styrofoam and other types of plastic every year. To find a solution, they joined the Unplastify Challenge , a global movement initiated by the Latin American social enterprise Unplastify and funded by the National Geographic Society, a nonprofit that seeks to foster environmental stewardship. What makes the program unique is its audience, design and scope. Teenagers, usually 15 to 16 years old, design and implement solutions to “unplastify” their schools, communities, neighborhoods and homes. In Singapore, the students decided to campaign for multi-use lunch boxes, winning them first place in the Unplastify Challenge 2026, the 12th such event of its kind. A garbage-strewn beach in Bali, Indonesia. Unless effective action is taken, it’s predicted that global plastic production will more than double over the next 15 years. Credit: Mariia Ploshikhina / Shutterstock In the eight years since it began, Unplastify has worked with over 3,000 students at 400 schools in 25 countries, mostly in Latin America, but also in Africa, Asia, North America and Europe. Together these students have come up with over 1,000 strategies, leading efforts to avoid an estimated 72 tons of plastic. In Chile, students have designed a biodegradable alternative to plastic glitter, thus avoiding four kilos of plastic in a single year. In Costa Rica, students have replaced plastic sponges with natural luffa. headline_hi: दीवारों पर काई उगाने वाला कंक्रीट
headline_en: Concrete that grows moss on walls
summary_en: A startup from the Netherlands has discovered a unique, eco-friendly technology. This Dutch company, named 'Respyre', has created a coating called 'Mosscrete'. It helps grow green moss naturally on concrete walls. This technology is based on research from Delft University of Technology. This moss does not need soil or irrigation to grow. The moss derives its nourishment solely from rainwater and moisture in the air. The fine roots of the moss stick to the surface without damaging the wall. The company has worked on eight different projects in Belgium and the Netherlands. This coating was applied to the wall of a warehouse in Kortrijk, Belgium. In Hoofddorp, Netherlands, it is being tested on a roadside wall. This technology will prove very effective in making bare city walls green.
source: The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News

lead.title: A Dutch startup is making concrete that grows its own moss
lead.summary: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Most building materials are designed to resist the elements, to stay sealed and unchanged for as long as possible. Respyre , a Dutch startup, is working from the opposite premise. The company has developed Mosscrete , a bioreceptive concrete coating that creates conditions for moss to grow directly on vertical surfaces, drawing moisture from rain and air without any soil or irrigation system. The science comes from research at Delft University of Technology , and since its commercial launch, Respyre has applied the technology across eight projects in Belgium and the Netherlands. How moss takes hold Moss doesn’t have roots in the conventional sense; it attaches to surfaces through rhizoids, tiny thread-like structures that cling to the material without penetrating or damaging it. Unlike a traditional green wall , which needs structural support for soil, a built-in watering system, and regular upkeep, Mosscrete sidesteps most of that. And because it’s applied as a coating rather than built in, it can go onto an existing facade just as easily as a new one. The material works especially well on blank or inaccessible walls where conventional planting isn’t an option, and Respyre has been using those spaces to test how the technology holds up under different real-world conditions. Eight buildings, different tests In Kortrijk, Belgium, 450 square meters (about 4,840 square feet) of a new industrial warehouse facade were coated with Mosscrete during construction and integrated with rainwater harvesting, keeping the whole system maintenance-free from day one. headline_hi: बंद होने के बाद भी खुली लाइब्रेरी
headline_en: A library open even after closing
summary_en: The Wyoming branch of East Central Regional Library in Minnesota, USA, has launched a new initiative called 'Extended Access'. Under this, people can enter even when the library is closed and unstaffed. A man named Michael Sayen works on his novel here on a computer. He shared that even on closed days, one can come here to work or find relief from the heat. Sayen has also found this facility useful for submitting important job applications and court documents. According to the library's executive director, Carla Lydon, this arrangement will allow even those people to use the library who cannot visit during regular hours due to work or family commitments. Such a facility is also running under different names in Utah and Nevada County, California.

lead.title: The Library Is Closed. Feel Free to Come In.
lead.summary: This story was originally published in the Daily Yonder. For more rural reporting and small-town stories visit dailyyonder.com . For Michael Sayen, visiting the local library after hours is a great way to get work done, or seek respite from the weather, regardless of what day it is. “We just had Labor Day, the library is closed all day. But if you have extended hours, you can come in and do the work, or cool down from a hot day or whatever you need to do,” Sayen said the day after Labor Day while working on a novel at the Wyoming, Minnesota branch of the East Central Regional Library (ECRL) in Chisago County. Sayen, who lives in nearby Forest Lake north of Minneapolis, adds that he has found after-hours access useful for filing time-sensitive job applications or court documents. Michael Sayen uses a computer at the Wyoming Giese Memorial Library to work on a novel. Sayen is a user of the Extended Access program at the Wyoming Library. Credit: H. Jiahong Pan/Daily Yonder The Wyoming branch library is home to a new ECRL initiative called “extended access,” which allows users to access a library branch when it is unstaffed. “We hope that it allows more people to use the facility, in particular those who may not be able to get to the library during otherwise limited hours due to work and family schedules,” ECRL executive director Carla Lydon wrote in an email. ECRL is one of a handful of rural library systems across the United States to offer such a service, increasing library access at a time when libraries are struggling for funding. How it works Extended access goes by many names depending on location. The Summit County Library in Utah calls it extended access hours .
